an3.70:1.3: This discourse, one of the key texts for lay practice in the canon, is fittingly addressed to the leading laywoman Visākhā ([an1.259:1.1]()).
an3.70:1.4: She was a busy woman taking time off work.
an3.70:1.5: “Sabbath”, ultimately from the Hebrew, is a weekly day of rest and worship in Judaism and Christianity. The _uposatha_ (Sanskrit _upavasatha_, literally “dwell close”) plays a similar role in Buddhism. One difference, though, is that the _uposatha_ is measured by the lunar calendar, so it falls on a different day each week. | In my monastic experience in north-east Thailand, the _uposatha_ was the major day around which the monastic lifestyle circled. Each _uposatha_, laypeople would come to the monastery, from local villages and towns, and some even from interstate, to offer food and share in the meal. They’d take the eight precepts in the morning and listen to a short Dhamma talk. Many would then stay in the monastery all day, resting, reading, meditating, or doing light chores such as sweeping. In the evening, there would be meditation and chanting in Pali and Thai, followed by a long Dhamma talk. On the dark and full moon fortnights, the monastics would gather to recite the _pātimokkha_ rules. Towards midnight, the activities over, Saṅgha and laity alike would settle in for all night meditation. Not all would make it, but many would. Then, around 4am, the community would rise and gather again for morning chanting. Towards dawn, the laity would tale five precepts once more and then disperse, while the monastics prepared for almsround.
an3.70:2.3: Curiously, there is no mention of the Brahmanical _upavasatha_, which was the original observance. This was the day of preparation before the fortnightly Soma feast day, on which the site for the fires was swept and prepared, and the sponsor of the sacrifice and his wife undertook vows of abstinence (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1). The sponsor “dwells close” to the sacred fire, to which the gods approach and thus dwell close to him (ŚB 2.1.4.1, 3.9.2.7). The current Sutta adapts the same meaning for Buddhism ([an3.70:6.6]()).
an3.70:3.1: _Nigaṇṭha_ (literally “knotless”) is a word for Jain ascetics, as _bhikkhu_ is for Buddhists. See Sūtrakṛtāṅga 14 for a description of the _nigaṇṭha_ from a Jain perspective.
an3.70:3.8: This is a misrepresentation of the Jain _digvirativrata_, the “vow of restraint in the directions” (Tattvārthasūtra 7.21). According to Jainism, every action has the potential to cause harm, even if unintentional. Traveling puts the lives of small creatures at risk with every step; today, this harm is monstrously amplified in the creatures left dead by cars, planes, and ships. Jain devotees could take an optional vow to reduce this harm by restricting travel, selecting landmarks or setting limits beyond which they would not go. Of course, within these limits they would still practice the qualities of love, compassion, rejoicing, and equanimity that Buddhists call the immeasurables (TS 7.11), and implement the five aspects of non-harming of all creatures: control of speech, thought, and movement; care in placing objects; and inspection of food (TS 7.4).
an3.70:3.11: This reflection occurs three times in the Pali. At [an4.185:7.2]() it leads to the dimension of nothingness for a brahmin. It leads to the same attainment in a Buddhist context at [mn106:8.2](). Here it is said to be a Jain practice, which they understand as asking people to eliminate attachment by going naked. A similar reflection is found in the Jain Ācārāṅgasūtra: “I am alone, no one belongs to me, and I do not belong to anyone” (_ego aham aṁsi, na me atthi koi, na yāham avi kassai_, 1.7.6.1). There, as here, the saying is presented as a quoted formula. It is a reflection at the start of the hot season, when a mendicant should cast aside their old robes and go either naked or in one cloth. While male Jain ascetics of the Digambara sect do indeed go naked, this is not a practice enjoined on lay folk in general. It is possible that the practice changed, as the Ācārāṅgasūtra is considerably later than the Pali suttas. Or perhaps the passage here is an exaggeration.
an3.70:3.28: This again misrepresents the actual Jain practice (Tattvārthasūtra 7.34). On the observance day, a disciple is enjoined to inspect and take care to avoid harm in three respects: going to the toilet, taking any object, and spreading mats on the ground. They further vow to exercise respect and earnestness (_anādāra_), while undertaking mindfulness meditation (_smṛtyanupasthāna_)
an3.70:4.1: Here the Buddhist sabbath is described in terms of meditative and ethical practices. For the Saṅgha, it was also a day of gathering together for a communal recitation, thus adhering to the original sense of “dwelling close”. The meditations taught here focus on the recollections, and at [snp5.19:8.1]() to  recollect the Buddha is said to be like living close to him. Moreover, the undertaking of precepts is also done with the perfected ones in mind. Thus while the practices are individual, they maintain the sense of “dwelling close” in mind.
an3.70:5.2: The first act of one undertaking the Brahmanical _upavasatha_ is to dip their hand in a water vessel for purification (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1.1).
an3.70:8.2: _Cuṇṇa_ is a powder of predominately herbal composition.
an3.70:11.2: Text reads _usmā_ (“heat”), but the similar passage at ([sn22.89:12.2]()) has _ūsa_ (“saline soil”).
an3.70:14.2: Mirrors were made of bronze, so this is a method for polishing bronze rather than cleaning glass..
an3.70:19.1: What follows is the eight precepts, which are still undertaken by devoted Buddhists on the _uposatha_, or when staying in a monastery or on retreat. Called the “eight-factored sabbath” at [an8.41](). As with all Buddhist precepts, they are undertaken consciously and reflectively by one who understands what they are doing and why. There is no such thing as a “commandment” in Buddhism.
an3.70:19.3: The first and most important precept. It is not just the negative injunction to avoid killing, but also the positive injunction to have compassion for all creatures.
an3.70:21.2: “Chastity” is _brahmacariya_, literally “divine conduct”. Here it is used in the narrow sense of refraining from sex, but more commonly it has a broader sense of “spiritual life” ([sn42.7:2.6]()).
an3.70:22.2: This is the first of the four kinds of right speech. Just as the precept of not killing implies the positive injunction to live with compassion, the precepts on speech enjoin a positive and constructive use of speech.
an3.70:23.1: _Surā_ is brewed from grains with yeast ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pc51:2.1.2]()). _Meraya_ is made from flowers, fruits, or sugars ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pc51:2.1.4]()). _Majja_ is apparently a catchall. Together they correspond fairly well with the modern classification of alcoholic drinks as “beer, wine, and liquor”. See also Manu 11.94, Arthaśāstra 2.25, Suśrutasaṁhitā 1.45, Amarakośodghāṭana 3.6.
an3.70:24.2: The Brahmanical _upavasatha_ was a day of fasting, although even a text as early as the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.1.1.7–10) discusses the differing interpretations of the fast. Some recommend a total fast, as it would be unfitting to eat before the gods; although milk, it seems was still allowed (ŚB 9.5.1.1). Yājñavalkya in his subtlety, however, divined that this meant the food would in fact be offered to the departed ghosts instead. He solved the problem by allowing only such food as is not offered at the sacrifice, namely food gathered in the forest.
an3.70:25.2: Such sensual entertainments distract and excite the mind. This and the next three precepts encourage peace of mind for meditation.
an3.70:28.2: This famous list of the sixteen “great countries” (_mahājanapadā_) is one of the most important records of the political structure of the Buddha’s India. The idea of sixteen nations is numerological: sixteen is four (quarters) times four, signifying a massive abundance of territory in all directions. Hence the Zend Avesta begins with a description of sixteen Persian lands, of which two are shared with early India: the town of Varṇu ([an2.37:1.2]()), and the “seven rivers” of the Indus valley (_saptasindhu_, Rig Veda 4.28.1, etc.). | Of the many spelling variations, the trickiest to sort out is Vaccha. The Mahāsaṅgīti and Buddhajayanthi editions have Vaṅga, but this seems unlikely, as Vaṅga is another country (= Bangla), and it is in the wrong place in the list, which for the most part rises with the sun in the east and moves west (for this convention, see [dn19:36.2]()). The PTS edition has Vaṁsa, a reading that is also found in Sanskrit sources. The preferred term in Sanskrit, however, is Vatsa, which appears to also be the basis for some of the Chinese transliterations of this name.
an3.70:29.1: This is an example of the relativistic theory of time in Buddhism (see [dn23:11.1]()).
an3.70:34.4: This works out as 1600 × 30 × 12 × 16000 = 9,216,000,000 human years. Given that the duration of each ascending realm increases fourfold, it suggests that the next realm is 36.864 billion years. In [vb18:191.3]() the lifespan of Mahābrahma, from the full development of the first absorption, is one eon. See [mn83:11.4]() and note there.
an3.70:38.3: _Siṅgīvaṇṇa_, or else _siṅgīsuvaṇṇa_ ([an3.70:38.3]()), is gold from a mountain peak (_siṅgī_). Kauṭilya mentions a form of gold that is _śṛṅgaśūktija_, “occurring on mount Śūkti” (Arthaśāstra 2.13.3). The commentary to that passage says it had the color of red arsenic, so it was a rose gold. | The same chapter tells us that _kañcana_ (“lustrous gold”) is of high purity which may be alloyed for making jewelery.
an3.70:38.4: The commentary, deriving _haṭaka_ from “take”, says this is gold extracted by ants. This echoes a fable well-known in the West from Herodotus; it seems the commentaries were listening to the same tales. Perhaps the fable originated with the Himalayan marmot, whose leavings are in fact sifted for gold by locals. Alas, Kauṭilya also mentions _hāṭaka_ as a form of gold, and the root is rather Sanskrit _haṭ_, “shine”. See also _hāṭaka_ at [thig14.1:17.2]().
